items: Downgrade protection: transcript hash + version-fallback sentinel
Blocks an attacker forcing weak parameters
Renegotiation was a minefield: 2009 attack, triple handshake
TLS 1.3 removes it in favour of key update
ClientHello carries a key_share for the expected curve
So DH starts on message one, not message four
Everything after ServerHello is already encrypted
Only ClientHello and ServerHello travel in cleartext
Wrong guess: HelloRetryRequest, 2 RTT — the fallback, not the norm
Removed: static RSA, custom DH groups, RC4, 3DES
Removed: MD5/SHA-1 signatures, compression (CRIME), renegotiation
Forward secrecy is mandatory — every handshake is (EC)DHE
HKDF key schedule: separate handshake and application secrets
Resumption: PSKs in NewSessionTicket, replacing session IDs

blocks.title: The 0-RTT Trap
items: Early data rides the very first flight — zero round trips
Replayable: there is no server-side freshness proof
Idempotent GET only, never POST or transactions
No forward secrecy: protected by the stored PSK, not fresh DH

blocks.title: Middlebox Compatibility Mode
blocks.text: TLS 1.3 fakes legacy version fields and sends dummy ChangeCipherSpec records so broken inspection appliances do not drop the connection.

items: Binds a public key to an identity, signed by a CA
It is public data — nothing inside is secret
SAN is what browsers actually check
Chrome has ignored CN matching since 2017
A cert carrying only a CN simply fails

caption.text: Part 4 of DNS & TLS FIELD HANDBOOK. Four round trips happen before your browser sends a single byte of HTTP — and most outages live in those four. This handbook walks the whole path: DNS hierarchy, delegation, glue, TTL maths and the propagation myth, then TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 handshakes, X.509 chains, cleartext SNI and ECH. Ends with the mistakes that break both and the exact dig and openssl commands that find them.
